dispatch.dek: The Goose regular who published his own bot mishaps just put his name at the top of the Generalist Gaming public board.
dispatch.editorNote: Disclosure: Keith Tyser was a Team Turducken teammate of Loose Goose editor Mark Barney and of Son Pham in ARC-AGI-3. Barney and Pham co-wrote the team write-up cited here.
dispatch.headline: Keith Tyser grabs the arcade lead

image.alt: Keith Tyser’s yellow fish character sends a tiny wheeled arcade cabinet across the workshop floor.
image.caption: Keith Tyser sends his pint-size cabinet out for a test run. The place on his nameplate is from the public board at 20:18 UTC on 25 November.

sections.text: Keith Tyser barged into the arcade and took the high score. The leaderboard from Tuesday evening didn’t have his name on it. By Wednesday evening the Goose regular was in first place on the public board at 0.408, and Kaggle listed him alone on the team.

sections.heading: The mistakes he kept

image.alt: Keith Tyser in a circuit-board coat with a GPU cane. Behind him hang one gold, three silver and six bronze medals.
image.caption: Tyser’s career-card character, with a medal display based on his 30 October Kaggle profile.

sections.text:
Tyser helped with reinforcement learning on Team Turducken in ARC-AGI-3, where the team wrote that its training runs fell short of its base model on Kaggle. He also spent months at a very different sort of workbench, building agents to steer fleets, play Pokémon cards and run farms. He wrote up what broke. His Orbit Wars simulator ran fast enough to rack up more than a billion simulated transitions, but the bot he built by hand still beat the strongest model he trained. He sent the hand-built bot and took bronze. In Pokémon, a bug made his early submissions pick the first available option until he caught it. He took silver there.

Plenty of people will show you their medal case. Tyser will show you the busted parts on the bench.

sections.heading: Tyser’s medal record

image.alt: The back of Keith Tyser’s career card lists one gold, three silver and six bronze medals on his dated Kaggle profile.
image.caption: The reverse of Tyser’s career card, with his 30 October Kaggle profile tally and medal finishes.

sections.text: Tyser’s gold came in ROGII’s wellbore geology competition. His medal record also includes NeuroGolf, Pokémon and Kaggriculture.

sections.heading: The next cabinet
sections.text:
Generalist Gaming sends the same agent from one game to the next with its memory intact. Change the game and a move that worked a minute ago can be the wrong thing to try. The private leaderboard decides the finish.

Tyser has spent months finding out what his bots do when a game stops behaving the way he expects. Who can catch him on the public board?

previousReview.notes: Independent review of the corrections made by a separate Claude Opus 5.5 Medium corrections session; this reviewer did not write the story or the corrections. The corrections cited only the 00:34 UTC board for "Tuesday evening", but under the paper's UTC rule that read falls on Wednesday; I made the 24 Nov 21:08 UTC board the Tuesday citation and kept the 00:34 read beside it. I changed "By Wednesday afternoon" to "By Wednesday evening", since the 20:18 UTC read is evening in UTC (the old word came from Eastern time). Disclosure: the Team Turducken roster record lists Tyser, Mark Barney and Son Pham; the line now reads plainly. Copy: no banned words, no Eastern or AM/PM times, no says, the one closing question among the three stories, source titles plain and listed once. Cards: the Generalist Gaming and ARC-AGI-3 fronts are unchanged. Art and the unchanged sections (blog, Turducken write-up, medal record) rest on the prior review; the medal record and both medal images are dated 30 October and are not refreshed here, which the planned fresh-career rule will flag. The saved-board links point to the planned /news/boards pages; stage only after that page ships.
